How I noticed

Yesterday I said the next job was working out how many tables your library contains. Grouping the sessions by camera geometry and cloth colour gave EIGHT groups, which should have looked wrong to me immediately.

So I zoomed into the same corner of the table in three of those groups. Same grain in the wood. Same pocket leather, same braid. Same little diamond markers in the same places. Same plate on the rail. Same carpet. One table, photographed under different lights with the camera nudged.

What that changes

the cloth's green reading, same cloth every time
   your afternoon sessions      165, 166, 167

   across the whole library     165 to 230

That is a big swing for one piece of cloth, and it is not daylight - your brightest reading is late morning and your dimmest is mid-afternoon. It is which lamps were on.

The good news is that the app was already doing the right thing: it keeps a colour record per SESSION, which is exactly right for something that changes with the lighting. My plan yesterday - one record per table - would have collapsed everything into a single record and reintroduced the exact mistake I spent rounds 62 to 69 digging out of.

Cloth colour is now a cheap way to tell which sessions were lit the same way. Three of your unmeasured sessions match one of the two I have verified almost exactly - within one or two units. The idea

Three balls on your newer table - the green 6, burgundy 7 and black 8 - are never potted in that clip, so the trick I used yesterday (the ball that disappears IS the one you potted) cannot touch them. The averages came out beautifully clean. But what shows on the ball is the white circle the number sits in, not the number - from straight overhead the digit is on the curve of the ball and squashed to nothing.

I set out to stop the app ignoring a ball that is sitting right next to your hand. I could not do it honestly, so I changed nothing - and the reason is worth telling you, because I nearly fooled myself.

The problem

The app deliberately ignores whatever is inside your arms and hands, so a glove is never mistaken for a ball. A ball sitting beside you gets ignored along with it. That is why the red 3 spends six seconds as an estimate rather than something the app can see.

The obvious fix: only ignore a ball if it is actually COVERED, not merely close. To test that I needed two groups - balls the rule wrongly discards, and hands it rightly discards - and to check they look different.

Where I nearly went wrong

They did look different, in the wrong direction, which was suspicious. So I looked at the pictures. My "hands" group was mostly BALLS - a blue ball held in your gloved hand, a red one you were handling. I had built that group by asking which detections my notes did not list as balls, and my notes deliberately skip balls while you are moving them by hand.

So I was comparing balls against balls and would have reported a clean finding either way. The honest answer is that I never had the two groups I claimed to have.

images.caption: The 'moving ball' my score was penalising: a leftover estimate drifting across empty cloth at a speed no real ball reaches. There is no ball anywhere along that streak.

entries.html:
Yesterday I reported a small step backwards. I went to find out what caused it, and it turns out nothing did - the app had got slightly BETTER and one of my measurements was wrong.

                        what I reported      what it actually is
balls named while moving     99.3% -> 98.7%      99.3% -> 99.4%

What the measurement was doing

When the app loses sight of a ball it keeps a short estimate of where it probably went. My "balls named while moving" score was counting those estimates as if they were balls it could see.

Yesterday's fix stopped a leftover estimate from hogging a real ball's number. That was right - but it meant the leftover estimate now had no name, and my score counted it as "a moving ball the app failed to name". All eleven cases were the SAME estimate, drifting across the table at a speed no ball reaches, over empty cloth. You can see it in the picture: a streak with no ball anywhere on it.

Counting only balls the app can actually see, that score is 99.4% - slightly better than before yesterday's change, not worse.

Why I am telling you rather than quietly correcting it

This is the second time in seven rounds that one of my own scores turned out to be the problem rather than the app - the other was the cue ball being marked down for seven seconds while it sat in a pocket. Both were the same mistake: counting something that is not there as though it were.

It also means a reported regression deserves the same scrutiny as a reported win. If I had shrugged yesterday's number off as the price of a fix, the app would have carried a wrong score and I would have believed it.

Nothing about the app changed today.

entries.html:
I went to fix the last known tracking gap, measured it properly, and concluded the app is already right. Nothing changed today - which is the point.

The gap

On the newer clip there is about a second and a half where the app loses sight of the cue ball. It is sitting in the jaws of a pocket with your cue stick lying across it.

The app has a rule that anything it sees only faintly, right next to a pocket, is the pocket's leather rather than a ball. That rule exists because the leather was once being tracked as a ball for minutes at a time, inventing shots. Your cue stick lying over the ball makes the ball look faint, so the rule throws it away with the leather.

Why I did not "fix" it

The obvious fix is to let a faint detection through if it is the colour of a real ball. I measured that on both sides before writing any code:

the leather the rule correctly kills   nothing like any ball colour (277 cases)
the real cue ball under the stick      also nothing like any ball colour
one dark false detection               looks a lot like the black 8

With the stick across it the ball's colour is spoiled, so it resembles nothing - while a dark false detection resembles the 8 nicely. The "fix" would have let the false one in and still thrown the real ball out. So I wrote none of it.

What the rule is actually worth

On your pinned table it correctly discards 277 false detections at the pockets - I checked the pictures and they are empty felt. It costs 11 frames of one real ball. And even in those 11 frames the app does not lose the ball: it keeps following it, it just marks those moments as estimates rather than sightings.

I have written the measurement into the code beside the rule, so a future session does not "improve" it and quietly bring the phantom shots back.

My reference notes already record, second by second, which balls are visible - so the app's score now simply skips the moments when the cue ball is not on the table. entries.html:
A regression, reported the same as a win. I found why the app loses sight of balls, built the fix, and it broke something worse - so it is reverted and both your clips are back exactly where they were.

What I found

When you lean over the table, the app deliberately ignores anything inside your arm and hand, so a glove or a cue butt is never mistaken for a ball. A ball sitting right next to you gets swallowed by that same blanking, and the app is built to just coast the ball through it and pick it up again afterwards.

It allows six tenths of a second for that. You stand over a shot for far longer. Measured on both clips:

your pinned table, the red 3   ignored for 6.3 seconds
the newer table, the 7         ignored for 6.7 seconds

In both cases the ball is plainly visible in the video and the detector still finds it confidently - it is the blanking that removes it. So the ball simply disappears from the app for six seconds, and it happens precisely when you are down on the shot, which is exactly when the app should be working.

What I tried, and why it was wrong

I let a ball that is sitting still be coasted for eight seconds instead. It fixed the disappearing exactly as intended. It also broke four pots across the two clips - makes and misses went from perfect to 8 of 10 and 7 of 9.

The reason is obvious in hindsight and I should have seen it before running it: a potted ball is also a still ball that stops being seen. A ball rolling into a pocket slows down first, so its last moments look exactly like a ball sitting quietly - and my rule then left it sitting on the table for eight seconds, so the pot never registered.

Where that leaves it

Reverted, and both clips measure exactly as they did this morning - your pinned session still names zero balls wrong. The failure narrowed the problem usefully: the app has to distinguish "I cannot see this ball because YOU are standing over it" from "I cannot see this ball because it went in the pocket". The difference is whether your hands are over that spot, which the tracking part of the app currently is not told. Wiring that through is the next job, and it is the work I was trying to shortcut.

What I got wrong

I had recorded the two balls as being nearly the same colour - so close that no scoring could separate them - and excluded both. Measuring them properly, they are almost twice as far apart as I thought. The "closeness" was between the red ball and a bad sample: when I recorded the orange ball's colour I must have caught the edge of it, picking up cloth and shadow along with the ball. The number I wrote down does not match ANY ball on that table.

So a real capability sat switched off for nine rounds because of one contaminated measurement of mine.

How they are separated now

Not by colour at all, which was the trap. The order the balls are potted tells me exactly which balls are on the cloth at any second. The red 3 is potted at 2:01 and the orange 5 at 2:39, so in between there is only one of the pair left - whichever ball that is, it must be the 5. From there I follow that ball backwards through the video position by position, stopping if it ever becomes ambiguous. It never did: 1,756 steps back across two minutes, and its colour holds steady the whole way. The other warm ball is then the 3 by elimination.

Two earlier attempts failed before this worked, and both were my methods being sloppy rather than the idea being wrong.

The score on that clip reads 99.6% instead of 99.9%. Nothing about the app changed today - the test simply got 29% bigger and now includes two balls it had been letting through unexamined. A harder exam with the same result is better information, not worse performance.

entries.html:
The app can now show its working. Until today it recorded only the name it decided on, never the evidence behind it - so twice I have had to run special one-off investigations to answer "why did it call that ball a 13?". That question now answers itself on every run.

                          pinned session      new clip
shows the name its
own evidence supports          99.5%           99.4%
   of live sightings          34,246          43,358

Why this matters

There are five separate safeguards between what the app sees and the name it puts on screen - things that stop two balls sharing a number, stop a name flickering, stop one glimpse naming a ball. Any of them can override what was actually seen, usually for good reason. But none of them left any record, so when a name came out wrong there was no way to tell whether the app misread the ball or read it correctly and then overruled itself. Those are opposite problems with opposite fixes.

What it found - and I was wrong about this

I had written in the project notes that the app "discards correct readings". Measured across 77,000 sightings, the opposite is true far more often: the safeguards are mostly CATCHING bad readings, not throwing away good ones.

The clearest case is on the new clip. For 87 frames the app read a ball as the 3 and displayed it as the 5. The display was right and the reading was wrong - and I can prove it without relying on colour at all: the 3 was potted at 121.7 seconds, so a ball still on the table at 136-159 seconds cannot be the 3. It then leaves the table at 158.9, which is exactly when the 5 is potted. The picture below shows a plainly orange ball, which agrees.

The two problems I had generalised from were real, but they are the rarer direction. I should not have written the general claim from two cases.

A gap in my own scoring sheet

Those 87 frames sit in a blind spot: the red 3 and the orange 5 are so close in colour on that table that I excluded both from my reference sheet, which means my scoring never checks either of them. The pot order gives me a way to settle them that has nothing to do with colour, and that is next.

More than half of everything the app sees had never been checked by anything. It has been trusting a crude colour guess on 43-55% of the balls in every frame, and that - not the naming model - is where the made-up ball numbers came from. Both your clips now report zero invented numbers, a first.

What was actually happening

The app names a ball in two stages: a naming model reads it, then a check compares the ball against the real measured colours of your set and overrules the model when it is clearly wrong. That check only ran on balls the naming model had read. And the naming model reads far fewer balls than I assumed:

new clip     846 balls seen, 461 of them (54%) never read at all
pinned       790 balls seen, 339 of them (43%) never read at all

Every one of those fell back to a crude colour guess that nothing checked. The guess was handing out a "10" on a table with no 10, and an "8" on your pinned table, which has no 8. That is exactly the made-up numbers you have seen. The check now runs on those balls too - it already did while you were playing, it just never did when the app analysed a recording.

Your pinned session slipped by a tenth of a percent: one sighting of the purple 4 is now left unnamed instead of named. Against that, its naming of balls IN MOTION - the hard case - went up, and the new clip gained 1.3% and lost every single invented frame. I kept the change, but that dip is real.

What is left

One confusion remains on either table: the yellow ball against the yellow striped ball, ten frames on the new clip and two on your pinned one. Everything else on both tables is now named correctly in every frame I can check. Those ten are the frames where the stripe's band is turned away from the camera and there is simply less white to see.

entries.score: The stripe repair was live-path only and has never executed on a recorded clip; and the app publishes a ball name that 8 of 366 frames support.

images.caption: Top row: the frames where the app says 13. Middle: where it says 9. Same ball, same orange body and white band, only rotated - so one of those two names is simply wrong. Bottom: the plain orange ball it keeps getting confused with, which has no band at all.

entries.html:
A repair I built for your pinned table over six rounds turns out to have never run on a recorded clip in its life. It worked while you were playing and was skipped entirely when the app analysed the video afterwards.

The app fixes a ball's name in two steps: correct the stripe-or-solid bit, then correct the colour. The live path did both. The path that analyses a recording did the colour half only - so the stripe half has never executed on a single clip I have ever measured. Every scorecard in this campaign was taken with half the repair missing, and last round's fix to that exact code changed nothing at all, because the code could not be reached.

                     pinned session         new clip
shots found              10 of 10           9 of 9
makes and misses         10 of 10           9 of 9
pots to right ball         4 of 4           5 of 5
naming              99.6% -> 99.8%    97.5% -> 97.6%
invented numbers        none, still     151 -> 330 frames

The regression, stated plainly

Your pinned table improved on every measure. The new table did not: the app now invents the name "13" on 330 frames where it used to on 151. I have kept the change rather than undoing it, and the reason is the next paragraph - but that is a real step backwards on that clip and you should see it as one.

What is actually broken, and it is not naming

I followed that ball frame by frame through the twenty seconds where the app calls it a 13:

what the app SHOWS for it     13 on 330 frames,  9 on 36
what the evidence SAYS         9 on 143 frames,  1 on 130,
                               5 on 85,         13 on EIGHT

The app is displaying a name that eight frames out of 366 support, and ignoring the answer that 143 support. Whatever decides a ball's final name is not taking the majority of what it saw. That is the real defect, it sits after naming rather than in it, and no amount of improving the colour reading can reach it. It is the top of the queue now.

And a mistake in my own method

Partway through this I measured the naming chain against my reference sheet and it looked nearly perfect - 65 of 66. I said so. Then I measured the same ball over the same seconds at full frame rate and it was right 143 times out of 366. My reference sheet samples about one frame a second, on settled moments; it is a good yardstick and a badly misleading survey. The near-perfect number described my sampling, not your app.

entries.score: The striped ball is the 9 after all - 61 correct reads had been scored as errors. Naming on the new clip 93.3% -> 97.5% with no code change.

entries.html:
The app was right and I was wrong. The striped ball on the new table is the 9 after all - I had been marking 61 correct answers as mistakes. With my notes corrected and nothing changed in the app, naming on that session goes from 93.3% to 97.5%, which passes.

makes and misses         10 of 10        9 of 9

naming                      99.6%          97.5%

How I got it wrong

I compared the striped ball on the new table against the yellow striped ball on your pinned table. Next to that one it looks distinctly orange, so I recorded it as the orange stripe and spent two rounds trying to work out why the app kept insisting otherwise.

The comparison was the mistake. The two tables are lit differently, and on the new table the plain yellow ball ALSO looks amber. Put the striped ball next to its own table's yellow ball and they are obviously the same colour - which makes it the 9, because on a pool set the 9 is just the 1 with a white band.

I then ran the same test on your pinned session, where I already know the answer: it correctly identifies that table's stripe as the 9. A method that reproduces an answer you already have is worth more than one that merely sounds convincing.

This keeps happening, and it is worth saying plainly

That is the third time my own reference notes have been the fault rather than the app - once on your pinned session, twice on the new one. Every time the cause was the same: judging a ball's colour against something from a different table. I have written the rule into the notes so it is not repeated: compare a ball only against other balls on the SAME cloth under the SAME light.

What is actually left

Almost everything on that table is now named perfectly - the cue, the blue, the green, the black, the burgundy, the purple. The one remaining confusion is the yellow ball against the yellow striped ball, which are about as close as two balls can be on that cloth. That is the same pair your pinned session struggled with for six rounds before it was solved, so there is a known route.

entries.score: Silent NameError in the shot writer, fixed; plus why the striped ball still cannot be named, and a flaw in my own reference sheet

images.caption: Left: the yellow striped ball on your pinned table. Right: the striped ball on the new one, which the app also calls a 9. Their bands are about as far apart as two ball colours get.

entries.html:
Found a crash that has been happening on every single clip the engine has processed for eleven rounds, silently. Nothing was broken by it, which is why it went unnoticed - including by me, ten days ago.

The silent crash

The last line of the shot-writing step printed a summary: how many shots, how many were real strokes. When I reorganised that rule a week ago I forgot this one line, and it has thrown an error ever since. The error was caught by a safety net that logs "shot derivation failed" and carries on.

Everything still worked because that line runs AFTER all the shots have been written - so the shot list was always complete and correct. The only casualty was the summary itself. But an error thrown on every run is not something to leave lying around, and I had actually SEEN this message in an earlier round and talked myself into believing it was harmless. It was not harmful, as it happens, but I had no basis for that belief at the time.

The striped ball, measured properly

The app calls that ball a 9. A 9 is the YELLOW striped ball. I compared its stripe directly against the yellow striped ball on your pinned table:

your pinned table's 9      band colour reads pure yellow
the new table's stripe     band colour reads amber/orange
                           - about as far apart as two ball colours get

So the name is wrong, whatever the right one is. The machinery to fix it already exists and is well built - it reads the colour of the BAND across the ball rather than the ball as a whole, which is the right idea. It fired 698 times and every time concluded the app's answer was consistent, because the reference sheet for that table has no entry for the orange ball it would need to match against. I removed that entry myself two rounds ago for a good reason, and it turns out the two uses need different things.

Something I need to flag about my own reference sheet

When I named that table's balls from photographs, three of them - the gold, the red and the orange - are genuinely hard to tell apart on that cloth, and for those I went along with what the app called them because it matched what I saw. That is not an independent check. If the app mixes those three up in some systematic way, my scoring sheet would agree with it and I would never know.

The other seven balls were read from colour alone and are sound. I have written this down as something to fix before it is used to justify any change - those three need re-deriving from something the app never touched.

entries.html:
The app now learns each table's ball colours separately, instead of carrying one table's around forever. Naming on the new session went from 85.7% to 93.3%, and your pinned session did not move at all.

What was wrong

The app knows your pinned table's exact ball colours - that is what stops it calling your purple ball a 7 there. There was only ever ONE such set, and it described that table. On the new session it matched nothing at all, so the correction simply never ran, and the purple ball was called the dark red one in 25 places.

I tested that explanation before building anything: I temporarily gave the app the new table's colours and re-ran the clip. Naming jumped straight to 93.3% and the purple/dark-red mix-up vanished completely. Then I put the old ones back and built it properly.

the purple ball     66 of 111  ->  110 of 111
the dark red ball  126 of 151  ->  151 of 151
balls left unnamed         46  ->          1

Checked by eye on the exact frame that used to get it wrong: seven of the eight balls on the table are now named correctly.

The one that is still wrong, and why

The orange STRIPED ball is still called a 9 (the yellow stripe). This is not the colour data - I gave it the right colour and it made no difference. The correction has a line in it that only allows solid balls to be renamed, so a striped ball can never be corrected no matter what the app knows about it. That single restriction is the entire remaining gap on that session.

Fixing it means letting colour decide the FAMILY and the stripe test decide which of the pair - the gold 1 and the orange 13 are nearly the same colour but one is 3% white and the other 21%. My reference sheet already does exactly that and gets it right every time, so the method is proven; it just needs to move into the app.

Building a yardstick for a second table

Until today I could only check WHICH BALL the app named on your pinned session, because that check was hand-fitted to that table's six balls. entries.title: The stripe test was calibrated on a table with no stripes
entries.score: Measured why the orange striped ball reads as solid, and why no single threshold can fix it

images.caption: The striped ball in question, at four moments. About a quarter of it is white - unmistakable against the solids on that table, and still below a threshold measured on a session that has no striped balls.

entries.html:
Chasing the striped-ball problem to its root. The app's test for "is this ball striped" was calibrated on your pinned session, and your pinned session has no striped balls at all.

What the test actually does

It counts how much of a ball looks white. A striped ball is white at the poles with a colour band across the middle, so from overhead it shows a lot of white; a solid ball shows almost none. Below a third white it calls the ball solid; above about a half it calls it striped.

Measured on the new clip, ball by ball:

the orange striped ball     23% white
every solid ball on it       0 - 7% white
the cue ball                74 - 100% white

On its own table that striped ball stands out perfectly from its neighbours. And it still falls under the "one third" line, so the app declares it a solid - confidently - and then adjusts its number accordingly.

Why there is no quick fix

An orange band is darker than a yellow one, so less of it counts as white. The threshold came from 398 balls measured on your pinned session, where the only striped ball is yellow. Worse, on that table some SOLID balls reach 31% white - higher than this clip's stripe at 23%. So there is no single number that works for both tables. I tried a version that judges each ball against the others in the same frame; that does not separate them either.

What I did change is small and honest: the app now says "I do not know" instead of "definitely solid" for balls in that range. It made no difference to any score on either clip - which I am reporting rather than dressing up - but it stops a confident wrong answer from overwriting the naming model.

The real fix, and the order it has to happen in

The app already learns each table's colours - that is what stopped it calling your purple 4 a 7. The striped test needs the same treatment: learn what "striped" looks like on THIS table under THIS light, instead of carrying a number from somewhere else. But first the new clip needs its own per-ball reference sheet, or I have no way to prove a naming change helped rather than hurt. That is the next job, in that order.

Both sessions still read correctly at shot level - 10 of 10 and 9 of 9 shots, makes and misses, and every pot credited to the right ball. Everything left is naming.

images.caption: The ball I had wrong. It is an ORANGE striped ball - an orange band on white - photographed at four different moments. I recorded it as a yellow 9, so the app was marked wrong every time it read the stripe correctly.

entries.html:
Today I found that most of what I have been calling the app's mistakes on the new clip were mine. And I tried a fix for the rest, measured it, and threw it away.

I had the balls wrong

When I wrote up the new clip as a reference session I listed eight balls on the table. There are ten. I missed a dark burgundy ball sitting still in the same spot the whole time, and I mistook an ORANGE striped ball for a yellow one.

That mattered, because the app was being marked wrong for naming both of them correctly. Of the roughly 10,000 frames where I said it was inventing balls that do not exist, 5,739 were the app being right and my notes being wrong. The honest figure is about 4,270 frames, all of them one real mistake: the orange striped ball gets called the 9, which is the YELLOW stripe.

I rewrote the reference file, including how each ball was identified, so the next person - or the next me - can check it rather than trust it.

The real problem, now clearly stated

The app has no working idea of stripes on that table. Your pinned session has six solid balls and no stripes at all, so this has never once been tested. On the new clip the striped ball is unmistakable in the pixels - about a quarter of its surface is white, against almost none for every solid - and the app still calls it a solid ball's neighbour.

The fix I threw away

Balls bounce off cushions. The app predicts where a ball will be from where it was going - which is exactly wrong at a cushion, where the ball turns around. entries.html:
No score changed today. I spent the round finding out why one pot on the new clip is still scored a miss, and the answer was three layers below where I was looking.

What actually happens at 158 seconds

You strike the cue ball; it hits the orange 5; the 5 runs down and drops in the bottom-left corner. The app says no ball fell.

Yesterday I said the app "lost the ball in mid-roll". That was wrong. It did not lose anything - the two balls SWAPPED places in its head at the moment they touched. I checked by sampling the actual colour of the pixels under each tracked ball, frame by frame:

the ball it calls "the cue"    white ... then ORANGE, heading into the pocket
the ball it calls "the 5"      orange ... then WHITE, rebounding away

Each one followed the wrong ball out of the collision. So the pot happens on something the app thinks is the cue ball, and a cue ball going down a pocket is a foul, not a pot - hence "no ball fell".

And the swap starts earlier than that

The part that names balls gets BOTH of them wrong for a few frames while they are touching: it reads the white cue ball as "the 5" and the orange 5 as "the 3". Everything after that is the app faithfully following bad information - including a rule I added last week that says a ball's NAME should outrank its position, which here drags the 5's identity straight onto the white ball.

What I shipped, and what I threw away

I wrote two guards. One says a ball cannot suddenly become a differently named ball; I deleted it - it changed nothing measurable, and on this very case it would have made things worse by stopping the 5 from recognising itself while it was mislabelled. Names are the thing that breaks in a collision, so names cannot be what guards it.

The other says a ball cannot change colour, and that one I kept, because I could prove it works: instrumented at the exact frame, it correctly refuses the white ball and holds the 5 on the orange one. It does not fix this shot yet because the cue's own track reaches the orange ball first, and the guard deliberately stays out of the way of balls in flight. Widening it is the next job.

The new clip found two shots the app got wrong - and one of them I had already told you was fine. Correcting that first.

I was wrong yesterday

I said the app had missed no shots on the new clip. I checked the gaps between shots thoroughly, noted that a shot could also be hiding inside a stretch labelled "Table change", checked the long one - and stopped. The miss was in the short one I skipped.

At 62 seconds you play a soft, controlled shot: the cue ball rolls gently down the table into the blue 2 and pots it in the side pocket. The app called the whole thing a Table change and lost the shot AND the pot.

The reason is the kind of thing only a second table can show you. The app decides "was that a shot?" partly on how fast the cue ball moves, and the threshold was set from your pinned session where every single shot drives the cue at 691 pixels per second or more. This one peaks at 325. The number was never a rule about pool - it was a fact about one session. It is now set from both.

And a pot scored as a miss

At 158 seconds the orange 5 runs down the left rail and drops in the bottom corner. The app says "no ball fell". It is not a scoring mistake: the app follows the 5 for about a second and then loses it in mid-roll, and it has a deliberate rule that a ball it lost track of in open play is never claimed as potted. That rule is right. Losing the ball is the bug, and it is the same weakness that used to cut the trails short on your bench session.

entries.html:
The question I could not answer until now: does the app ever MISS a shot entirely? On the new clip, it does not - and I can finally prove that rather than assume it.

Why this was a blind spot

Every number I have ever shown you scores shots against a list I wrote by watching. That catches wrong calls. It cannot catch a shot the app never mentioned - if it is missing from the list AND missing from the app, there is nothing to compare. A clean report and a clean report with a hole in it look identical.

So I built something that does not ask the app anything. It flattens each frame to a top-down view of the cloth and compares it to the frame before, which sees balls rolling no matter what the app thinks. On the new clip: 28 separate bursts of movement, 12 during shots the app reported, 16 not.

Checking all sixteen

A struck ball on your table travels 691 to 2974 pixels a second - measured across all ten shots of the pinned session. The fastest ball inside any of those sixteen bursts is 332. None of them is a shot.

I watched the three strongest anyway, because an argument is not a look:

151.0s   fastest ball 332 px/s   you walk up and get down on the shot
 56.8s   fastest ball 193 px/s   same - addressing, balls all still
143.5s   5.5s, the most movement of any  you chalking and moving the
         of them, but only 44 px/s       cue over the cloth

All three are the cue STICK sweeping over the table while every ball sits still. Then one more gap in my own reasoning: a shot could hide inside a stretch the app labelled "Table change", which my test skips by design. So I watched the long one at 26 seconds too - the balls change position completely between frames, you moving them by hand and pushing them with the stick. A genuine rearrangement.

Where that leaves the new clip

3 pots      all three correct, checked frame by frame (yesterday)
8 shots     none missed, checked against raw movement
2 setups    the long one confirmed a genuine rearrangement
5 misses    NOT yet checked - next

First run on a clip I have never touched. It held up - all three pots called correctly on a different day, different rack, different lighting - and it immediately caught a bug the pinned session never could.

The cold test

Everything so far has been measured on one session, the one I have been grinding on for weeks. That proves the rules fit THAT table. So I picked a clip from a different day that appears in none of my notes - 3.3 minutes, session-20260823-185550 - ran it, and then watched every pot myself:

48.9s    "potted the 1 into the top-right"       a yellow ball drops   RIGHT
121.7s   "potted the 3 into the bottom-right"    a red ball drops      RIGHT
138.1s   "potted the 4 into the bottom-right"    a purple ball drops   RIGHT

What it caught

That third one originally read "potted the 1". The app had the right answer and printed the wrong one: internally it had credited the 4, and the sentence you read was built by a completely separate piece of code that worked out which ball vanished on its own - and got a different answer.

On the pinned session those two always agreed, so the disagreement was invisible for weeks. A new table made them differ within three minutes. The sentence now simply reports what the engine decided, instead of deciding again.

This is the third time in three days I have found the same shape of mistake: one fact with two owners. First the scoring report had its own private idea of what counts as a shot; then the shot description had its own idea of which ball fell. Each one hid a correct answer behind a second, worse one. I have started hunting the rest deliberately instead of waiting for a clip to expose them.

Also fixed: the app on a fresh machine

The colour references that let the app tell your purple 4 from your 7 lived only in a local settings folder. On any new machine - a reinstall, a second PC - they would be missing, ball naming would quietly get worse, and nothing would say why. They now ship with the app itself, and if they ever go missing it says so out loud instead of silently guessing.

Being straight about what I checked

I verified all three pots frame by frame. I have NOT yet verified the five shots it called "no ball fell", the two setups it labelled Table change, or - most importantly - whether it MISSED any shot entirely. A missed shot is invisible to every number I have, because those numbers only score shots something already told me about. The last fault, and how it fell

The one thing left was the 13-second setup being scored as a shot. The app was meant to catch that by seeing your hand over the table, and I spent a while convinced the hand-detector was blind. It is not - I was wrong about that, and about a second thing too, and both corrections are worth stating.

The detector DOES see your arm: about 2-3% of the table covered, against 0.4% for an empty table. What it cannot do is connect the arm to a ball, and the reason is almost funny: a ball being carried is hidden by the hand carrying it. So it has no position for the app to follow, so there is nothing for the app to mark as "in a hand". It was looking for a ball that by definition it could not see.

So I stopped trying to see the hand and used something the app can always measure: nothing on a pool table moves until the cue ball gets there. Across your whole session that splits the cases cleanly:

all ten real shots     the cue moves FIRST, by 0.07 to 0.43 seconds
the 13s setup          the cue moves LAST, 2.90 seconds behind

You placed the 3, the 4 and the 9 by hand and only touched the cue ball six seconds later. No shot works that way. A ten-to-one margin, no hand detection needed.

The fix worked and the scoreboard kept failing it

Worth admitting: after that change the app's own shot list was correct - the setup properly labelled a Table change - and my scoring report went on saying "1 fake shot". The report had its own private copy of the "what counts as a shot" rule, written months earlier, which had never been told about the new test. So the thing that judges the work was judging by different rules than the work itself. There is now one copy that both use.

What this does and does not mean

This is one clip - the one I have been grinding on for weeks. It is now clean, which means the rules are right for this table, this light, this session. It is not proof the engine is reliable in general. The next test is a clip I have never tuned against, scored blind, and I expect it to find things. That is the point of it.

Round 50: a ball that left the table two and a half minutes earlier came back and stole a live one. Your 208-second shot is scored correctly again, and the bench now has exactly one fault left.

It held the 2 for eleven frames, died inside the pocket, and the app scored that as "potted the 1". Meanwhile the same shot's own trail list had the 2 right there on the table. One shot entry, contradicting itself.

entries.html:
Round 49, and this one came straight out of your question. Asking what "99.6% named correctly" meant led to a purple ball that the app deleted from existence for 82 seconds - while every number on the scorecard said it was being tracked perfectly.

What the metric was hiding

Yesterday's answer: the headline divided by the moments the app HAD a ball, so the 88 checks where it had nothing were left out. I added the unforgiving version - right divided by every check, blind included. It read 91.4%, below the 95 bar. So I went and looked at those 88 moments.

81 of the 88 were the same ball, the purple 4, in one unbroken stretch from 19 seconds to 101 seconds. Not occluded, not blurred - sitting still on open felt in plain view. The app's nearest tracked ball was 264 pixels away.

The cause: a ball measured against the wrong ruler

The app finds a ball, then converts its position to a flat overhead view. A ball sits a couple of centimetres ABOVE the cloth, so the app corrects for that height. The bug: it applied the correction to the ball's centre but NOT to the second point it measures the ball's WIDTH against - so the width came out as a distance between two different maps.

The error leans one way. On one side of the room balls measured too small, on the other too big. The purple 4 was on the small side:

what the detector saw     a ball, 0.87 confidence, correctly read as "4"
its measured width        8.72 pixels
the minimum accepted      8.94 pixels

Thrown away by two tenths of a pixel, every frame, for 82 seconds. The proof it is fixed is not the ball reappearing - it is that every ball on the table now measures the same size. Before, widths across one frame ranged 8.7 to 14.2. Now they range 12.0 to 12.9, against an expected 12.4. That is what the overhead view was always supposed to give.

The 13-second setup is still called a shot. I fixed one real bug there (the cue's speed was being measured across a moment where its label jumped to a different object, reading 2920 px/s when the true figure is 213), but it was not the whole cause.

entries.html:
Round 48. You asked what "99.6% named correctly" actually means - the honest answer is below, and it is less flattering than the number. Also: the app had a whole subsystem that has never once run on a recorded clip.

What that percentage really counts

There is a truth file built from the PIXELS, not from the app: one snapshot per second for 220 seconds, five balls each, so 1,096 individual checks. Each check asks "the app has a ball tracked here - did it put the right number on it?" Every check lands in one of four buckets:

right                                                 1,004
wrong  (called it another ball)                           3
unnamed (tracked it, never named it)                      1
no track (truth says a ball is here, app has nothing)    88

The headline is 1,004 divided by 1,008 - right, wrong and unnamed. The 88 "no track" checks are not in that denominator. So the honest sentence is: of the moments the app had the ball at all, it named it right 99.6% of the time. In another 88 moments - 8% of every check - it had nothing there to name.

That is not hidden on purpose (the line prints the 88), but 8% blind is a bigger hole than 0.4% misnamed, and worse, the headline number goes UP as tracking gets WORSE, because losing a ball shrinks the denominator. I have put a second, unforgiving figure at the top of the queue: right divided by ALL 1,096 checks, which today is 91.6%. Both will show in the app.

The three genuinely wrong ones are all the same pair - the yellow 1 and the yellow-striped 9. Those two really are near-identical yellows; measured, 7.3 units apart in colour space.

A subsystem that never ran

The app has a recovery pass for balls the detector loses to motion smear. I found it has NEVER worked on a recorded clip - not once, on any session. It needs each ball's measured colour, and the offline path skipped the one place that colour is sampled. So it sat there, called every frame, unable to consider a single candidate.

Switching it on immediately did two good things - the purple 4 went from 134 of 136 to a perfect 136, and naming rose to 99.6% - and one bad thing: it made the engine three and a half times slower. Measuring where the time went: 66% of it was the recovery pass, and 87% of THAT was hunting for phantom tracks that have no name at all. It was searching hardest for things that were never balls.

Two limits fixed that, both from what the feature is actually for - it only hunts a ball it can NAME (a nameless smudge has no identity to keep), and it waits for a ball to be genuinely gone rather than blinking for a single frame. Plus it now reuses its background instead of rebuilding a 1000x1000-pixel median from fifteen frames on every single search.

entries.html:
Round 47: your @85 bank is fixed, and my last explanation of it was wrong. The app was not losing sight of the ball. It could see the 3 the whole time and had already read the number off it - it just handed the ball to the wrong track, by two pixels.

What actually happened

The moment you strike a ball, the app has to decide which of the balls it is already following this new blip belongs to. It does that by predicting where each ball should be and taking the closest match, within a limit.

That limit was generous for a ball sitting still and TIGHTER for a ball that had started to move - which is exactly backwards. A struck ball goes from nothing to fifteen feet per second in two frames, so the prediction is at its worst precisely when the limit was being tightened. On your bank:

the 3's own detection, already labelled "3"   50.1 pixels away
the limit the app allowed it                  47.7 pixels

Out by two and a half pixels. So the app started a brand new, nameless track on the real ball and left the 3's track drifting on a stale guess. The trail you saw was drawn between those two - a straight line across a path the ball never took. The limit is now a floor that cannot be taken away mid-shot.

Two more of the same family, found by measuring

A dead blob reached across the table. A nameless smudge parked in one corner pocket since 17 seconds in grew its reach a little every frame it went unseen, until it could claim something 496 pixels away in the OPPOSITE corner - and published it as a "5", a ball your table does not have. Its reach is now capped.

Your 170.6s long pot was credited to nobody. The app had correctly read "1" on the moving ball. The 1's own track was 32.8 pixels from it - but that same parked smudge sat 28.6 pixels away and won on distance alone, by four pixels. The 1's track died, the ball rolled into the pocket nameless, and a real pot could not be attributed. A name now outranks four pixels: the read is evidence, distance is only a guess.

pots attributed      4/4           fake strokes            0

entries.html:
Round 46: your @85 report, diagnosed by stepping through the shot. The missing piece of the 3's trail is not a drawing problem - the app loses sight of the ball during the fastest part of its travel and then draws a straight line across the gap.

What the numbers show

t=85.54   the 3 at (259, 376)   at rest
t=85.69   the 3 at (240, 384)   creeping - the app lagging, not the ball
t=86.14   the 3 at (211, 396)
t=86.29   the 3 at (490, 622)   360 pixels in a seventh of a second

A real ball does not do that. What actually happened: the 3 was struck, crossed a third of the table while the detector could not see it - a fast ball smears and loses contrast, so the model returns nothing - and was picked up again on the far side. The trail then joins the last place it was seen to the first place it was seen again with a straight line.

So the missing transient tail you spotted is the app quietly drawing a path the ball never took. It is honest about the endpoints and invents the middle.

Why I am not patching the drawing

I could break the line where the jump happens, which would stop showing you a fictional path. But that gives you a gap, not the tail you actually want. The real answer is for the app to SEE the ball during that half-second, and there is already a feature for exactly that - the blur-recovery pass that finds smeared balls the detector misses. I restored it six rounds ago and it currently finds nothing, even on the clip it was originally built for. That is the next thing to fix.

This is the first defect I found the way you find them - by stepping through the shot and looking, rather than reading a metric. Every number on the scorecard says this shot is perfect: detected, outcome right, the 3 named correctly, the pot credited to the right ball. A fabricated trail is invisible to all of them.

Round 38: started merging the two engines into one. The first real step is done - there is now one kind of "tracked ball" in the code instead of two - and the practice clip scores identically, which is the proof it changed nothing it should not have.

What I did

The replay side and the live side each had their own idea of what a tracked ball is. The replay one carried six fields; the live one carried fourteen, including velocity and the position history that draws the trails. Two shapes for one idea - and that kind of split is exactly what has been producing the campaign's worst bugs, because a fix applied to one shape simply does not exist for the other.

There is now one. The replay tracker publishes the same rich object the live app already understands, and the private duplicate is deleted. I also gave it the three controls the live app drives its tracker with, so the swap itself is now a small change rather than a rewrite.

The practice clip scores exactly as before - every shot, every outcome, every pot, same naming - which is what I wanted from a structural change: no improvement, no regression, just less duplication.

Honest scope, because it is bigger than it looks

I had hoped to finish the swap today. Looking properly, the live tracker is wired into more than the pipeline: a blur-recovery feature reaches directly into its internals, and four test files pin behaviour it bought from real incidents on your table. Deleting it wholesale would throw that history away.

So the order is: make the new tracker satisfy the contract (today), swap the live path behind a measured before-and-after, port the blur-recovery hook, move that incident history onto the surviving tracker, and only then delete the other file. I would rather tell you it is three or four rounds than promise one and break something you use while playing.

On piping me the live feed

Good idea, and worth shaping now: I do not watch video continuously - I look at frames. What actually found every real bug in this campaign was targeted looking. So rather than streaming everything, the version I would argue for is that the engine flags its own suspicious moments - a moving ball with no name, a name changing while a ball sits still, a pot credited to nobody, high confidence on something it should not be sure about - and I review that queue as it arrives. Tens of frames a session instead of thousands, and pointed at exactly where the app is already unsure.

It is also worth doing after the engine swap rather than before, or I would spend the session re-finding faults that are already fixed on the replay side.

The thing that had been hiding underneath

Three rounds running I tried to fix the striped 9 by improving what the app sees. Every attempt failed, and each one failed in a suspiciously identical way. Today I stopped looking at what it sees and looked at what it is allowed to change its mind about.

There was a rule saying a ball that is not moving cannot become a different ball. It exists for a good reason - a resting ball flickering between two names is horrible - but it was written as an absolute. A resting ball's name could never be revised, no matter how much evidence piled up against it. Worse, it threw that evidence away as it arrived.

entries.html:
Round 32: found exactly why the striped 9 still gets called "1", tried the two obvious fixes, and both cost more than they gained. Your app is unchanged at 89% - but the diagnosis is now exact.

Why the 9 goes wrong, precisely

The 9 is misnamed in one unbroken stretch: from 157 seconds to the end of the clip. It does not drift there - the name flips in a single moment at 156.3, while the ball sits perfectly still.

Here is what happens in those few frames. The trained model reads that ball correctly as the 9 - it does so in 114 out of 114 checks across that whole period. But each frame, every model reading gets handed to exactly one ball, nearest first. At 155.8 the yellow 1 rolls past the 9 on its way through the shot, and the 1 is closer to the 9's own reading than the 9 is. So the reading gets given away, the 9 is left with nothing, and it falls back on the crude colour rule - which sees "yellow" and says "the 1". Six frames of that were enough to outvote it permanently.

Fix one: stop the colour rule from voting

If the crude rule is what poisons it, take its vote away when the trained model has not spoken. Result:

  • the striped 9: 141/221 to 219/221 - essentially fixed
  • the purple 4: 136/136 to 0/136 - destroyed

It turns out the colour rule is the only thing naming your purple 4 correctly; the trained model misreads that one. Net effect 89.2% down to 83.7%. Reverted.

Fix two: teach the colour rule about stripes

Instead of silencing the rule, repair its one blind spot - it cannot tell a solid ball from a striped one, which is the entire 1-versus-9 problem. I have a measurement that separates them cleanly on your table, so I wired it in.

Result: 59.4%. The 3 and the 9 started swapping names. Far worse, reverted immediately.

What this tells me

Both attempts treated the symptom - the wrong guess. The actual problem is upstream: the 9's own correct reading is being taken away from it by a ball passing nearby. The model never stopped knowing what that ball is; the app just keeps handing its answer to somebody else.

So the next attempt aims there instead: remember, for a moment, what the model last read at a given spot. A ball sitting perfectly still that was read as the 9 two frames ago should not be re-labelled "1" by a colour rule just because a neighbour borrowed its reading. That is a narrower change than either of today's, and it does not touch the purple 4.

Two failed attempts, both reverted, both measured rather than guessed - and the target for the next one is now specific instead of speculative.

entries.html:
Round 30: found both root causes of the naming problem, and both fixes work. Together they take naming from 76% to 89% correct. They are not shipped yet, because they knock one shot out of alignment - that is the only thing left between here and landing them.

Cause one: the app was overruling its own expert

There are two things that put a number on a ball. A trained model whose entire job is reading ball numbers, and a crude colour rule for when that model has nothing to say. The engine had the priority backwards: the colour rule won, and the trained model's answer was thrown away whenever the rule had already guessed.

For your striped 9 that is fatal, because the colour rule sees "yellow" and says "the 1" - it did so in 43 out of 43 checks. The trained model reads that same ball correctly as the 9 in 71 out of 72. Its correct answer was discarded on every single frame.

Letting the expert win: the 9 goes from 0 out of 221 to 141 out of 221, and the "9 called 1" error - 154 sightings - disappears completely.

Cause two: a name that wandered for 76 seconds

I traced the ghost from last round all the way through. One track's life:

t=  10.9   correctly the yellow 1, near the bottom rail
t=  32.2   follows the 1 into the bottom-right pocket - the ball is potted
t=  45.4   re-appears 12 seconds later, across the table, still called "1"
t= 109.2   re-attaches to the RED 3 - which then answers to "1" to the end

The cause is simple: a track was never actually deleted. When a ball disappeared, its track went dormant but stayed on the books, still eligible to grab any new ball that appeared - and the longer it had been missing, the wider it was allowed to reach. So a potted ball's name went looking for a new home.

Retiring a track once its ball has genuinely left the table - into a pocket or off the bed - fixes it. The red 3 goes back to 188 out of 189, and it stays fixed with the 9 fixed too.

The red 3 collapses the moment the careful path is connected, and none of the follow-up fixes touch it. (The colour references and the shaky-detection rule did earn their keep on other counts - together they took the invented numbers from 302 frames down to 38 and restored the shot outcomes to 9 of 10 - but they are not what breaks the 3.)

Chasing it to the actual cause

I asked the naming code directly what it thinks the red ball is. It answers "3", on every frame, and it is not a close call: the colour sits 14.5 units from the 3's reference and 147 from the 1's. So the part that reads balls is right.

Then I replayed the very same video frames through a fresh copy of the tracker. It also says 3, correctly, the whole way through. So the tracking logic is right too.

Both are right, and the finished output still says "1". The difference is history.

The bug, in plain terms

Your yellow 1 was potted 33 seconds in. Its track - the app's memory of "this is the 1" - did not die with it. At 110 seconds you hand-placed the red 3 on the table, and that leftover memory latched onto the new ball. From that instant to the end of the clip, the red 3 answers to "1", while the naming code underneath keeps saying "3" and is ignored.

The same thing explains the ball I told you about last round: the striped 9 has been wearing the name "1" since long before that, which is why it scores 0 out of 221. One stale name, two balls wrong.

So this is not a recognition problem at all. It is an identity problem: a name must not survive the ball it belonged to. When a ball is potted, its name should be released, and a ball that appears in a new place should have to earn a name rather than inherit one.

Where things stand

Everything is reverted; your app is exactly as it was, at 76.0% named correctly. Nothing shipped today, and nothing on your phone changed.

But the target is now precise for the first time in this campaign. I have spent several rounds trying to fix naming by improving how balls are recognised, and the recognition was never the problem. Next round goes at identity continuity - releasing a name when its ball leaves the table, and making a re-appearing ball prove who it is. Why the scoreboard needed fixing first

Last round I made a change that raised every naming number I track - and also started calling your red 3 a "1". The scoreboard reported a clean sweep, because it only ever asked two questions: did this ball get a name? and is that name one of the balls on the table? Calling the red 3 a "1" answers yes to both.

So today I built the missing measurement: is each ball called by its own name? It works out the right answer from the picture - each ball's colour, and for the two yellows, how much white the ball shows - and never looks at what the app thinks. Then it compares, ball by ball, and reports which balls get mistaken for which.

I checked the new yardstick by eye before trusting it. The image below is that check: four moments from your practice clip with the truth drawn on. All 23 labels are right, including the empty stretch after 170 seconds where the yellow 1 has been potted and is not yet back on the table.

What it found, immediately

per ball : 0: 221/221   1: 66/85    2: 156/156
           3: 187/189   4: 136/136  9: 0/221
confusions: 9 called "1" x154

Your cue, the 2 and the 4 are perfect. The red 3 is very nearly perfect. But the striped 9 - the ball sitting in the middle of your table the whole session - is never named correctly. Not once. It is called the "1" in 154 of the checks and left blank in the rest.

The old number said "75.7% of moving balls named". The honest number is 76.0% named correctly - and far more usefully, it says exactly where all the damage is. It is not spread thinly across every ball. It is one ball, failing completely, plus a bit of the yellow 1 that gets caught up in the same confusion.

Why this matters for what comes next

entries.html:
Round 27: I found out why none of the naming work has been landing. The app has been carrying two different sets of rules for reading ball numbers, and the good one was switched off.

The discovery

There are two pieces of code that decide which ball is which. One is the careful one: it checks a ball's colour against measurements from your table, repairs the common stripe/solid mix-up, and can name a ball that the model failed to read at all. The other just takes the model's raw guess.

The replay engine was using the raw one. Every naming improvement built over the past several rounds lives in the careful path, which the engine never calls. That is why my last two attempts to improve naming changed the score by exactly zero - I was fixing code that does not run.

I proved it by asking both about the same pixels: shown the striped 9, the careful path answers "9" with confidence; the engine's output called that ball "1" in 4,613 frames.

What happened when I connected the good one

Real gains, immediately:

  • Ball naming 75.7% -> 80.0%
  • Pots credited to the right ball 2 of 4 -> 3 of 4
  • The striped 9 correctly named 9 in 6,684 frames, instead of being called a "1" or nothing at all

You can see it in the picture below: the ball marked id4 = 9 is the striped ball that sits in the middle of your table all session. It has never once been named correctly before today.

Why I threw it away anyway

Look at the same picture again, at the red ball at the top. It says "?". Counting across the whole clip, the red 3 was being called "1" in 1,843 frames. I fixed one ball's name and broke another's.

A wrong name is worse than no name, so the whole change is reverted and the clip has been re-processed back to where it started. Nothing on your phone changed.

The part that actually matters

Here is the uncomfortable bit. My scorecard could not see that regression. It measures whether a ball has a name and whether that name is a number that exists on the table. Calling the red 3 a "1" passes both tests - 1 is a real ball on this table, and the ball did get named. The scorecard reported a clean sweep while the app was confusing two balls.

I only caught it because I looked at the picture.

So the next job is not another naming attempt. It is fixing the measuring instrument to check names against the right answer, ball by ball. Until it can tell "named correctly" from "named", every naming result I report to you - including today's 80% - is unreliable. That is the second time in three rounds the yardstick has been the problem, and I would rather find those than keep scoring against them.

Two smaller findings, both measured

  • The stripe/solid test was blind on your table: all 20 labelled crops of the striped 9 registered as solid, because the test only looks at a ball's middle - and a stripe's white is at its edges. Widening the window separates your solids (at most 0.21) from the stripe (at least 0.42) with clear daylight between.
  • The colour reference file still holds entries from 15 August for balls that are not on your table - a 5, a 6, a 7, an 8. The phantoms match those stale entries, which is where the invented numbers come from. Removing them cut invented-number frames from 302 to 56.

entries.html:
Round 26: chased the last missed pot, tried a fix, measured it, and threw it away. Here is what the app actually believes.

The picture below is the app's own belief drawn on your table at 140 seconds. Green circles are balls it has named, and it gets five of six right here - the 3, the 4, the 2, the yellow 1 and the cue.

Two things are wrong in that same picture, and they are the whole story of where we are:

  • id4 has no name (orange "?") - that is the striped 9, the ball that sits in the middle of the table and never moves all session. The app sees it perfectly well but cannot read which ball it is.
  • id7, bottom-left, is a ghost - a circle marked "est" (estimated) sitting on the pocket leather with no ball underneath it.

The one remaining missed shot, explained

The long pot at 170.6 seconds is the last outcome the app gets wrong. I traced it. The app does track that ball into the pocket: it runs to 14 pixels from the pocket centre - well inside the pocket - travelling at 3,000 pixels a second, and then disappears. That is as clean a pot as exists in this clip.

It scores nothing because the app never learned which ball it was, and there is a deliberate rule that an unnamed ball dropping into a pocket does not count. That rule exists for a good reason: earlier, a gloved hand lifting balls out of a pocket faked a make. So the missed pot is not a pot-detection problem at all. It is the naming problem wearing a different hat.

The fix I tried, and why it is gone

I found a second, real flaw on the way: a filter that requires an unnamed object to travel 250 pixels before it counts as a ball. It measures that distance over the object's entire life, so a ball that sits still for three minutes and then makes one short run gets judged on the wrong evidence. It was deleting the potted ball.

I removed it. The score got worse - strokes found dropped from 10/10 to 9/10 and outcomes from 9/10 to 8/10 - and the missed pot still did not score, because the naming gate above is the real blocker. So it is reverted. I am reporting it because a fix that measures worse is as much a result as one that measures better.

A correction to my own last report

Last round I told you 30% of what the app sees is not a ball. That number was taken before the app's own filters run. After filtering, phantom objects are 0.1% of what actually reaches the tracker (25 frames out of 34,821). The ghost in the picture is real, but it is rare, not rampant. I should have measured at the right place the first time.

Where this leaves us: everything now points at one thing - reading ball numbers. It blocks the last missed pot, it blocks pot attribution (2 of 4), and it is the 9 sitting there unnamed. That is the next job, and I know what it needs: telling solid balls from striped ones by how much white they show, which measures cleanly on this table (solids at most 0.10, stripes at least 0.19).

entries.html:
Round 25: the scorecard itself was wrong. I found it by looking, and fixing it moved the score from 8/10 to 9/10 without touching the engine.

Everything the app does gets graded against a "truth file" - a list of what really happened in the practice clip, written down by eye. Today I checked that list against the actual pixels for the first time. It had three real errors.

1. One ball was wearing three different names

The truth file said a yellow 1 and an orange 5 were both on your table. There is no orange ball. I sampled the colour of every ball the app finds across the whole clip - 1,534 detections - and not one of them is orange.

What actually happens: a single yellow solid ball gets potted, retrieved, tossed back on, and potted again. The old truth file called that one ball the "9" the first time it fell, the "1" in the middle, and the "5" the second time it fell. Three names, one ball.

2. The app was being punished for being right

The real 9 - the yellow one with the white stripe - never moves once. It sits at the same spot in all 111 samples from 18 seconds to 236 seconds. The old truth file said it was potted 32 seconds in. So every time the app correctly reported "the 9 is on the table", the scorecard marked it wrong.

3. A pot that never happened

The truth file recorded a pot at 130 seconds. Watching it at half-second resolution, the yellow ball rolls down to the bottom-right rail, comes back, and settles in the middle of the table - where it sits for the next 14 seconds. Nothing fell. The app said "no pot" and the app was right.

What this changes

Correcting the list - not the engine - moved outcomes from 8 out of 10 to 9 out of 10. Real pots on this clip: four, not five.

I want to be plain about what this does and doesn't mean. It does not mean the engine is fixed. It means some of what I have been chasing for the last few rounds was a phantom in my own measuring stick, and I was tuning against it. The one real remaining outcome failure is a genuine miss: the long pot at 170.6 seconds, which the app does not see.

Also found: 30% of what the app "sees" is not a ball

The same colour census turned up three fixed objects the detector reports as balls in hundreds of frames - the leather of the bottom-left pocket, a pale mark on the felt, and a dark object at the table edge. Together they are 462 of 1,534 detections. That is the next target.

One more thing I fixed about my own work

Two of the training examples I labelled last round were labelled "5". They are the yellow 1. I made exactly the same mistake the original watch made - calling that ball orange from a small, low-detail view. Corrected. It is a good argument for the rule you set: look at the actual picture, at full size, every time.

Round 24: last round's alarm was a false one, and looking at a full frame proved it.

I stopped mining yesterday because some training frames showed six balls where I thought seven were on the table - which would have taught the app that a real ball is background. Today I drew every box onto the full picture and looked.

The frames are complete. Every ball actually on the felt has exactly one box around it, including your orange 5 at the bottom-left. The 'missing' balls were simply balls that were already potted - not misses. The picture below is your table at 166 seconds: six balls, six boxes, plus one circle on the pocket leather that stays deliberately unlabelled.

I also tried filling the supposed gaps from the tracker's own memory. That was worse: it drew second boxes on balls that were already found - two circles on the same red, two on the same yellow. Reverted.

What this means: the 115 labelled balls are sound, and the part of the app that FINDS balls is doing its job. The failure is purely in reading which ball is which - exactly what the training data addresses. Training runs next round.
